whatShame.title: What shame is, and what guilt is
whatShame.lead: Guilt says "I did something bad". Shame says "I am bad". The whole path begins with this difference.
body: Guilt is about an act: a concrete thing you can name, repair or apologise for. It pulls towards action. Shame is about the whole self: "that's what I'm like", "something is wrong with me". It pulls towards hiding, disappearing, going silent. Tangney and Dearing's research shows guilt-proneness goes with empathy and repairing relationships, shame-proneness with depression, anxiety and anger.

In practice both often come together: a small act and a large "I'm hopeless". That's why the path asks every week "what is this shame about?" and separates three things: a deed (repair), an event that happened to you (care for yourself) and a demand that may not be yours (check it).
The point is not to stop feeling shame. The point is to recognise it sooner and know what to do with it, instead of letting it steer.
sources: Lewis 1971; Tangney & Dearing 2002; Kim, Thibodeau & Jorgensen 2011

notYourFault.title: Where shame comes from (not your fault)
notYourFault.lead: Shame is an alarm of the social threat system. Nobody chose their brain or their history.
body: Humans survived as a species thanks to the group. Losing acceptance used to be a real danger, so the brain has a built-in alarm that goes off when we feel we're losing our place among others. That alarm is shame. It fires fast, before we can think, and sets off old strategies: hide, attack yourself, attack others, look away.

Compassion-focused therapy calls this the "tricky brain": the system we were given and the history that tuned it are not our fault. What we do with it next is our business. Self-compassion isn't a reward for good behaviour. It's a muscle you train, as with a physiotherapist.
That's why the path starts with recognising and with the body, not with correcting thoughts. The alarm has to settle a little first; only then can another voice be heard.
sources: Gilbert 2009, 2014; Gilbert & Procter 2006

compassParts.title: Four parts that take the wheel
compassParts.lead: The Hider, the Critic, the Aggressor and the Avoider. Each protects. None of them is you.
body: Donald Nathanson described four automatic reactions to shame: withdrawal, attacking yourself, attacking others and avoidance. In parts language (IFS) each is a protector: a part that once learned to shield you from the pain of being seen. The Hider doesn't want you seen. The Critic gets ahead of other people's criticism so it hurts less. The Aggressor pushes others away before the feeling of smallness can hurt. The Avoider moves the feeling itself out of the way.

Once the reaction has a name it stops being "that's what I'm like" and becomes "my part took the wheel". Someone in you is left who can hear it out and stay. That's what the unblending sentence in your shame response teaches, and every entry in Moments.

Honestly: IFS is a frame here for understanding and talking with yourself. The evidence for the path's effectiveness comes mainly from compassion-focused therapy, the Mindful Self-Compassion programme and chairwork.
sources: Nathanson 1992; Schwartz 2021; Earley & Weiss 2013

threeSystems.title: Three emotion systems
threeSystems.lead: Threat, drive, soothing. Shame sits in the first. Warmth towards yourself needs the third.
body: The compassion-focused therapy model describes three emotion-regulation systems. The threat system looks for danger and responds with fear, anger, shame. The drive system chases reward and achievement. The soothing system handles calm, safety and connection; closeness, a warm voice, touch and a slow exhale switch it on.

In people with strong self-criticism the soothing system is often hard to reach: warmth towards yourself feels foreign, sometimes frightening. That's why in this path the soothing breath, the safe place and the compassionate image come before thinking. You can't argue the threat system down. You can settle it with the body, and only then speak.
A longer exhale than inhale, a hand on the heart, a calm tone of voice towards yourself: these aren't decorations of the exercises, they're the switch between systems.
sources: Gilbert 2009; Matos et al. 2017; Petrocchi, Ottaviani & Couyoumdjian 2017

whenWarmthHurts.title: When warmth hurts
whenWarmthHurts.lead: If sadness, anger or emptiness follows kindness to yourself, that's not a mistake. It's a door opening.
body: Chris Germer calls it "backdraft": let air into a closed, hot room and the fire flares. Let kindness into yourself and sometimes old pain flares: "where was this when I needed it?" It comes as tears, irritability, the thought "this isn't for me", pain in the body or the urge to abandon the exercise.

It's normal and common. It doesn't mean you're doing something wrong; it means the exercise reached where it was meant to. The rule: always practise at a level you can bear. If it's too much, close for today: return to the breath, to the safe place, to an ordinary activity that does you good. Every inward practice has a "Too much for today" button. Using it counts as practice too.

Resistance has its words too: "it's weakness", "I don't deserve it", "I'll get lazy", "I'll become dependent on it". Each of these voices protects against something. It's worth naming them rather than fighting them. If the pain after exercises doesn't pass or grows, see the card "When it's too much for self-help".
sources: Germer & Neff 2019; Gilbert, McEwan, Matos & Rivis 2011

actEventDemand.title: Deed, event, demand
actEventDemand.lead: Three answers to "what is this shame about?" and three ways forward: repair, care, check.
body: A deed: there was a real breach and it can be repaired. I forgot to call back, I criticised someone in front of people. Shame may be glued on ("I let the people close to me down"), but the core is the deed, so repair closes it. An event: there's no deed to repair. Failure, rejection, loss, illness. The answer is caring for yourself like a friend this happened to.

A demand: shame is guarding a rule that may not be yours or isn't fair. "Men don't cry at work", "after all these years I should know this". The test is simple: would you hold someone you like to this demand, and would you say they should be ashamed of it? If not, it's someone else's demand. The answer: check whose it is, phrase a fair one and do one thing against the unfair one.
Dialectical behaviour therapy calls the same thing checking the facts: justified shame leads to repair, unjustified shame to opposite action, which means not hiding.
sources: Tangney & Dearing 2002; Linehan 2015

readingProgress.title: How to read your progress
readingProgress.lead: More entries at the start is good. There are no streaks here. A week without moments is a quiet week, not a gap.
body: Progress on this path shows in three pictures from Moments. The first shows which part took the wheel week by week. At the start the bars grow because you start noticing; that's progress, not deterioration. Later what counts is how often no part took the wheel for good.

The second picture is the share of moments where you did anything instead of the reaction: a breath, naming, a sentence, contact. Every attempt counts, even an hour late. That fraction should grow slowly. The third picture is "when I notice": the share of moments noticed as they happened or shortly after. When it grows, the response has a chance to work.

The scale measures (SCS-SF and FSCRS) show the direction of change over time, not a verdict. The effects of such programmes are often delayed: in studies the difference often appeared only after two months. That's why the path comes back to you eight weeks after it ends.
sources: Neff & Germer 2013; Halamová et al. 2018; Breines & Chen 2012

criticProtector.title: The critic protects (and how to thank it)
criticProtector.lead: We don't silence the critic. We change the method it uses.
body: Self-criticism has two functions: correcting ("keep your standards, improve") and persecuting ("you deserve punishment"). People hold on to the critic because they believe it motivates and protects against others' criticism. Research says otherwise: after failure, kindness to yourself increases the wish to improve, and attack kills it. In compassion training groups the correcting function stays; only shame as its fuel goes.

Paul Gilbert compares it to two teachers. One points out the mistake with encouragement, looks forward, speaks about the specific behaviour, builds on what went well. The other condemns, looks back, speaks about all of you, threatens. Both want you to improve. Only the first one works.

That's why in week five you ask the critic: what are you afraid would happen if you stopped? Usually the answer is: that they'll reject you. That concern can be respected. The method can be changed. The sentence "thank you for keeping watch, I'm driving now" does exactly that.
sources: Gilbert, Clarke, Hempel, Miles & Irons 2004; Gilbert & Procter 2006; Breines & Chen 2012

notIndulgence.title: Compassion is not indulgence
notIndulgence.lead: The most common resistance: "I'll get lazy". The data say the opposite. And compassion has a fierce side too.
body: In Breines and Chen's experiments, people who treated themselves with compassion after a failure studied longer and were more willing to repair mistakes than those who shored up their self-esteem or distracted themselves. Compassion doesn't lower standards. It removes the fear that keeps you from approaching them.

Kristin Neff describes two sides of compassion. The tender one comforts, validates, keeps company. The fierce one protects, sets boundaries, says "enough", motivates. For someone who hears a voice of contempt inside, warmth alone is often not enough. They also need someone who will take their side. That's what the "Defending voice" exercise and the tasks teach: one "no" without explanation, head up, a sentence without "sorry".
Self-compassion isn't excusing yourself. It's what lets you look at your own mistake without running from it.
sources: Breines & Chen 2012; Neff 2021; Whelton & Greenberg 2005

outOfHiding.title: Out of hiding
outOfHiding.lead: Shame says disappear. Being seen by someone kind heals it.
body: Shame lives in hiding. Every time you hide, it confirms there was something to be ashamed of. That's why the last weeks of the path are small exposures to being seen: stay a minute longer, ask a "stupid" question, show unfinished work, tell one safe person about something you're ashamed of.

Dialectical behaviour therapy calls this opposite action: when shame doesn't fit the facts, do the opposite of what it says. Instead of lowering your eyes, lift them. Instead of softening your voice, speak fully. Instead of hiding, say it. Brené Brown calls the last move "speaking shame" and points out that another person's empathy is what disarms shame most effectively.

The behavioural experiment in week seven tests a concrete prediction: "if they see the real me, they'll reject me". A small, safe situation, the prediction written down, then the result. Usually the gap between what you expect and what happens teaches more than a week of talking to yourself.
sources: Rizvi & Linehan 2005; Brown 2006; Bennett-Levy et al. 2004

whenTooMuch.title: When it's too much for self-help
whenTooMuch.lead: This path helps with ordinary shame. Some things need a person, not an app.
body: Some signals mean it's worth pausing the path and talking to a professional: shame tied to violence, abuse or another serious injury; memories that return against your will, with a loss of contact with the here and now; thoughts of hurting yourself or a sense that you deserve punishment; pain after exercises that doesn't pass but grows; long weeks without energy, sleep or joy.

That's not a failure of the path or of you. Compassion programmes are effective and safe for most people, but in studies the most deeply ashamed most often dropped out on their own because the programme "looked disappointed". There's none of that here: you can pause the path, come back to it in a month or start over.
If you need to talk now, in Poland the 24-hour crisis helpline for adults is 116 123. In an immediate threat to life, call 112.
sources: Saraiya & Lopez-Castro 2016; Northover et al. 2021; Cai 2024

angerPause.title: A pause that leaves room to choose
angerPause.lead: Anger can be a signal. You can practise how you respond to it.
body: Think of a small, everyday situation. How do you recognise rising tension? You may speak faster or clench your jaw. In your pause plan, connect that signal with one simple action: a quiet moment, a comfortable breath or an explained break. Then return to your own words through “My plan”. You do not need to remember the whole exercise.

If the conversation is safe, suggest when you can return to it. After the break, you can say what happened, what you need and what you are asking for. A calm request does not guarantee agreement. This path invites you to notice your own action: was there a little more choice? You do not need to feel calm immediately or persuade the other person. One saved moment is enough to explore another response later.
sources: NHS — Get help with anger: https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/feelings-symptoms-behaviours/feelings-and-symptoms/anger/

angerSafety.title: When support is needed
angerSafety.lead: Understanding anger does not excuse hurting someone.
body: This path is a place to practise responding to everyday tension. It does not replace help when there are threats, violence, damage to things or concern that someone may be hurt. At that point, stop the conversation and prioritise safety. If there is immediate danger, contact local emergency services. Do not wait to complete the next step in the app.

If anger regularly affects your life or relationships, speak with a professional about suitable support. You can share your notes, but you do not need any notes to ask for help. After hurtful behaviour, you can name the specific action and take responsibility for it without attacking yourself. The other person has a right to distance, to decline a conversation and to take their own time. A repair task never obliges them to reconnect or forgive.
sources: NHS inform — Problems with anger self-help guide: https://www.nhsinform.scot/illnesses-and-conditions/mental-health/mental-health-self-help-guides/problems-with-anger-self-help-guide/

anxietySmallSteps.title: An attempt, not a test
anxietySmallSteps.lead: A small step can matter even when anxiety is still present.
body: On your ladder, choose a situation that is safe but brings anxiety. Write down what you want to do and what you fear. Start with a manageable version: one question, a brief conversation or a minor decision. Repeating it offers a chance to learn about the situation. You do not have to move up with every attempt. You can return to the same rung or make the step smaller.

Afterwards, notice what actually happened and what you were able to do. Your anxiety level is one piece of information, not a grade for the whole attempt. Reducing unnecessary reassurance does not mean stopping medication, ignoring medical advice or removing real protection. Do not choose activities involving genuine danger. If safety is unclear or attempts feel overwhelming, discuss them with a professional. Your map should help you choose a step, not force you to take it.
sources: NHS — Facing your fears: https://www.nhs.uk/every-mind-matters/mental-wellbeing-tips/self-help-cbt-techniques/facing-your-fears/

anxietyWorry.title: Giving worries some room
anxietyWorry.lead: Not every concern needs an answer right now.
body: Worry time is an invitation to return briefly to your notes. During the day, you can write a thought in one sentence and bring attention back to what you are doing. You do not need to remove the thought or win an argument with it. If it returns, you can return to your activity again. Choose a time that fits your day and is not just before bed.

Looking at a note, ask: is there a concrete action within my reach? If so, choose one small step. If not, you can leave the question unresolved for now. Do not postpone urgent responsibilities or dangers until worry time. If anxiety regularly limits daily life, seek professional support. Panic, OCD and trauma call for an individually tailored approach; this path does not replace that support. You do not need to finish these exercises before asking for help.
sources: NHS — Tackling your worries: https://www.nhs.uk/every-mind-matters/mental-wellbeing-tips/self-help-cbt-techniques/tackling-your-worries/
NHS — Get help with anxiety, fear or panic: https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/feelings-symptoms-behaviours/feelings-and-symptoms/anxiety-fear-panic/

angerRumination.title: Rumination keeps anger going
angerRumination.lead: Anger you chew over does not fade. It grows.
body: When you return to the situation in your mind, you replay what someone did and what they should have done. Every replay turns the tension up, as if it were happening again, and offers ever sharper versions of the same story. In research it is rumination, not anger itself, that best predicts the next outburst: not that you got angry, but how long you carried the anger.

Instead of fighting the thought, give it one of two exits. If it concerns something within your influence, write down one step and return to it at a chosen time. If not, notice the addition (“he does it on purpose”) and return to what you are doing right now. The worry tree, the thought record and a small step on the matter do exactly that. You do not have to stop thinking, only stop circling.
sources: Sukhodolsky, Golub & Cromwell (2001). Development and validation of the Anger Rumination Scale. Personality and Individual Differences, 31, 689–700.
Saini (2009). A meta-analysis of the psychological treatment of anger. Journal of the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law, 37, 473–488.

angerNeed.title: Anger defends a need
angerNeed.lead: Behind anger stands something that matters: a boundary, respect, fairness, rest.
body: Anger does not come from nowhere. It appears when something important was crossed or something you need was missing: respect, predictability, rest, honesty. An outburst says this indirectly, so the other person hears an attack, not a need, and defends instead of listening. A request says the same thing directly and leaves the other side room to answer.

In “A need and a request” you name the fact without judgement, the feeling, the need and one request that can actually be met. There is no guarantee the other person will agree. There is a fair chance they will hear you, and you know what you wanted before the anger drowned it out. In Moments the same list of needs waits under every entry, so you can name it calmly when there is no one left to ask.
sources: Rosenberg (2015). Nonviolent Communication: A Language of Life (3rd ed.). PuddleDancer Press.
NHS inform — Problems with anger self-help guide: https://www.nhsinform.scot/illnesses-and-conditions/mental-health/mental-health-self-help-guides/problems-with-anger-self-help-guide/

angerRepair.title: Repair breaks the loop
angerRepair.lead: After an outburst comes shame, after shame tension, after tension the next outburst.
body: An outburst rarely ends with the outburst. Guilt or shame remains, and they raise the tension from which the next one comes easily. Some people start blaming themselves at this point, some keep blaming others; both keep the loop going. Repair breaks it: you acknowledge a specific action, without explaining it away with the whole situation, and propose what comes next.

Repair does not require the other person to accept the apology at once. They may need time or not want to talk at all; that is their right. What counts is that the matter has been named and you no longer have to carry it. If the situation is not safe, stepping out of it can be the repair. The letter to yourself after a hard moment does the same towards you: kindness and responsibility in one sentence.
sources: NHS — Get help with anger: https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/feelings-symptoms-behaviours/feelings-and-symptoms/anger/
Saini (2009). A meta-analysis of the psychological treatment of anger. Journal of the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law, 37, 473–488.

anxietyUncertainty.title: Room for the unknown
anxietyUncertainty.lead: It is not about certainty. It is about being able to act without it.
body: Checking, seeking reassurance and reading one more review bring relief for a moment. A moment later the uncertainty returns, and with it the need for another check, because the relief taught you that it cannot be borne without one. Over time the relief gets shorter and the checking more frequent. The problem is not the unknown itself but the belief that it has to be removed before anything can be done.

Experiments with a small unknown work the other way: you choose a minor decision without real risk, leave it without the last check and watch what happens. Usually not much, and if something, it can be lived with. It is the experience, not the persuasion, that changes how you relate to uncertainty. That is why on this path you write the prediction down before an attempt and what really happened after it.
sources: Dugas & Robichaud (2007). Cognitive-Behavioral Treatment for Generalized Anxiety Disorder: From Science to Practice. Routledge.
NHS — Get help with anxiety, fear or panic: https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/feelings-symptoms-behaviours/feelings-and-symptoms/anxiety-fear-panic/

anxietyLearning.title: What a small attempt teaches
anxietyLearning.lead: A drop in anxiety is not the goal of the attempt. What you learn is.
body: For years it was thought an attempt worked when anxiety fell during it. Today we know what matters more is whether the prediction came true. If you feared you would not bear it, or that everyone would see, and you bore it and nobody reacted, the attempt worked, even if the anxiety stayed high to the end. The brain learns from the gap between what it expected and what happened.

That is why you write the prediction down before the attempt and what really happened after it. Different situations, different times and different people teach more than repeating one and the same. High anxiety during the attempt does not cancel the learning, and a drop in anxiety is not a condition of success. Genuine safety precautions stay: a seatbelt and a medicine your doctor prescribed are not safety behaviours.
sources: Craske, Treanor, Conway, Zbozinek & Vervliet (2014). Maximizing exposure therapy: an inhibitory learning approach. Behaviour Research and Therapy, 58, 10–23.
NHS — Get help with anxiety, fear or panic: https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/feelings-symptoms-behaviours/feelings-and-symptoms/anxiety-fear-panic/

anxietySafety.title: Safety behaviours and safety
anxietySafety.lead: Not everything that calms you is a safety behaviour.
body: A safety behaviour is something you do mainly for momentary relief: asking the same question again, a phone call “just in case”, sitting by the door, preparing an answer to every possible question. It brings relief and at the same time suggests the situation was dangerous and that you only survived it thanks to the precaution. That is why the anxiety returns next time at the same strength.

Medication, medical advice and genuine safety precautions are something else. Do not give them up as part of this path and do not make treatment decisions without a professional. If you are unsure which group something belongs to, ask: am I doing this because the situation requires it, or because otherwise I cannot bear the uncertainty? On the anxiety map you write down only the second group, and at first you only notice it.
sources: NHS — Get help with anxiety, fear or panic: https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/feelings-symptoms-behaviours/feelings-and-symptoms/anxiety-fear-panic/
Craske, Treanor, Conway, Zbozinek & Vervliet (2014). Maximizing exposure therapy: an inhibitory learning approach. Behaviour Research and Therapy, 58, 10–23.
